slides.0.title: Viticulture in depth and climate change
slides.0.subtitle: Marginal-climate risks, adaptation and sustainability
slides.1.title: Training, density and ripeness management
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Training systems the specification allows
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The INAO specification limits pruning to Chablis, Cordon de Royat, Guyot and Vallée de la Marne (Meunier only); pruning is therefore part of the law rather than a personal style, and it caps buds per vine and so yield potential
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Density is set by spacing
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The rules set spacing, not vine counts: rows ≤ 2.00 m, vines 0.70–1.50 m apart, the two together ≤ 3.00 m. In practice densities of roughly 8,000 vines/ha or more are common (an approximation, not a legal text). High density lightens each vine’s load and pushes roots to compete downward
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Why ripeness has to be “just right”
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Sparkling base wine wants high acidity, modest sugar and low phenolics: at least 9% natural alcohol and 143 g/L of sugar (specification). Pick too late and acidity and finesse go; too early and the fruit is green. Much of the region’s technique is about holding fruit in this narrow window
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Hand harvest of whole bunches is mandatory
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Whole-bunch picking and delivery to the press are required, so mechanical harvesting is effectively impossible (see Level 2). Labour, timing windows and weather risk therefore become part of both cost and style
slides.1.content: Level 2 gave the rules; this lesson asks how growers manage risk and ripeness within them.
slides.2.title: Weather and biological hazards
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Spring frost
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The first marginal-climate risk. Chardonnay buds earlier and is the most exposed; Meunier buds later and tends to escape spring frost (Level 1). Wind machines, heating and pruning timing help but never fully insure
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Mildew and humidity
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Cool, damp seasons raise downy and powdery mildew pressure; organic and biodynamic growers rely on copper and sulphur, which must be reapplied after rain washes them off (Decanter, 2023). This is also the motivation for disease-resistant varieties
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Heatwaves and scorch
slides.2.highlights.2.content: In summer 2019 Glannes recorded 42.9°C, the highest ever measured in Champagne (IWC Insight, 2019). Heat causes scorch, lower yields and sugar–acid imbalance; poor flowering and frost that year hit Chardonnay especially hard
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Hail and yield volatility
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Hail, frost and mildew make actual yields swing from year to year, which is exactly why the reserve system and the marketable yield exist: good years top up the reserve and poor years draw on it (Level 2)
slides.2.content: Each hazard maps to an institution or a style choice: frost and mildew point to varieties and protection, yield swings point to reserve wine.
slides.3.title: Climate change: earlier harvests and falling acidity
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Markedly earlier harvests
slides.3.highlights.0.content: IWC Insight (2019), citing CIVC data: over roughly 30 years harvests began about 18 days earlier on average, potential alcohol rose 0.7% vol, total acidity fell 1.3 g/L and mean temperature rose 1.1°C, while rainfall stayed near 700 mm a year. These are 2019-article figures; they are dated here and kept out of the quiz
slides.3.highlights.1.title: August starts are no longer rare
slides.3.highlights.1.content: IWC records an 18 August 2003 start, breaking the 20 August 1822 record, with further August starts in 2007, 2011, 2015 and 2018. An LVMH researcher (Polytechnique Insights) cites three August harvests in ten years. Both are single-source statements, used here as trend illustrations only
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Acidity, pH and nitrogen
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Falling acidity and rising pH reduce freshness and ageing backbone in the base wine; LVMH researchers also note that must nitrogen has declined since the 1980s, and IWC quotes producers on a shorter flowering-to-harvest span (about 100 days in the textbook, about 92 recently, 80–85 in 2019). These are observations by producers and researchers, not a uniform CIVC statistic
slides.3.highlights.3.title: The stylistic dilemma
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Riper fruit means a fuller, less austere wine but also less acid, so dosage levels, whether to run MLF and when to pick all become stylistic decisions (developed in ch-l3-2 and ch-l3-6). In Champagne climate change is not just “getting hotter” but “how to keep the acidity and tension sparkling wine needs”
slides.3.content: Read the figures with their dates and sources: the specifics come from articles around 2019 and from producers; the direction of travel (earlier, riper, lower acid) is what to learn.
slides.4.title: Adaptation strategies and sustainability certification
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Adjustments in the vineyard
slides.4.highlights.0.content: IWC quotes Philipponnat: harvest earlier and accept higher ripeness, higher canopies, wider rows, tilling or grassing between rows to restrain vigour, less nitrogen to lower pH, and in the long run slower-ripening clones and rootstocks. This is one house’s view, not a regional consensus
slides.4.highlights.1.title: A new variety: Voltis
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Voltis, bred by INRAE and Germany’s JKI, resists downy and powdery mildew and was approved for trial at the end of 2022: up to 5% of a grower’s vineyard and 10% of any blend, with a trial of about ten years (Wine Spectator). It is a “new variety”, separate from the eight traditional ones. In 2023 blind tastings with nearly 700 experts, blends with 5% Voltis were seen as rounder, simpler and more ready to drink (as reported)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Certification and herbicides
slides.4.highlights.2.content: The CIVC says over 60% of the region’s vineyards hold some certification (Viticulture Durable en Champagne, HVE, organic or biodynamic; a Decanter article from 2023, with no date given for the figure), with a goal of full certification by 2030. On herbicides, the specification bans pre-emergence products between rows (Level 2); the CIVC once aimed at zero herbicide by 2025, a goal Curtis MW reports was removed from its website in autumn 2022, so it is an aim rather than a mandate. Percentages and timelines move, so they stay out of the quiz
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Rules need flexibility too
slides.4.highlights.3.content: LVMH researchers argue that INAO rules should allow more flexibility so houses can experiment without risking downgrade (Polytechnique Insights). This is an industry position: the region’s tradition and quality assurance rest on strict rules, so any loosening (varieties, pruning, harvest dates) trades protecting style against adapting to climate — a classic MW essay theme
slides.4.content: Answer framework: hazard → effect on style → available tools (viticulture, winemaking, varieties, regulation) → trade-offs and costs.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is the most direct climate-change trend in Champagne?
A. Later harvests and higher acidity
B. Earlier harvests, higher potential alcohol and lower total acidity
C. Much higher rainfall and less mildew
Figures vary by year and source, but the direction is consistent: earlier, riper, lower acid (IWC Insight citing CIVC data).
Which statement about Voltis is correct?
A. One of the eight traditional varieties, usable in 100% blends
B. Permitted only for still wines
C. A mildew-resistant new variety, up to 5% of the vineyard and 10% of any blend
Voltis was approved for trial at the end of 2022 as a new variety, separate from the traditional ones and still in a trial of about ten years.
Which of these is a hard INAO rule for the vineyard?
B. Must be machine-harvested to cut costs
D. Whole-bunch harvest, no irrigation, no pre-emergence herbicides between rows
These three come from the specification (Level 2); organic is not mandatory and certification shares are industry aims.
